notes.claim: UK low-voltage supplies are declared at a frequency of 50 hertz and a voltage of 230 volts between the phase and neutral conductors at the supply terminals, unless otherwise agreed in writing.
Low voltage in building supplies is described as 400 V three-phase and 230 V single-phase; these are nominal voltages.
Sine, cosine and tangent are ratios of sides of a right triangle: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent.
In similar right-angled triangles the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides stay in the same proportion, so adjacent over hypotenuse is the same however much the triangle is enlarged.
For a right-angled triangle, trigonometry is used when a question involves two sides and an angle.
In a conduit offset bend, the offset depth is the side opposite the bend angle, the distance between bends is the hypotenuse and the horizontal run is the adjacent side.
The offset multiplier is the cosecant of the bend angle, 1 over sin: sin 30 degrees is 0.5 giving 2.0, and sin 45 degrees is 0.7071 giving 1.414.
The multiplier method is an approximation because it does not account for the arc of the bend itself (the source says the difference is negligible for most field work up to about 30 degrees).
Scientific calculators used for trigonometry should be in degrees mode, according to Bitesize.
Angles are measured as parts of a full turn, which is 360°; a quarter turn, 90°, is a right angle (added for i1's opening screen).
An obtuse angle is between 90° and 180° (added for i1's opening screen).
Angles that add together to make a right angle are called complementary angles (added for i1: the two non-right angles of a right-angled triangle).
An inverse function takes the output and does the opposite to get back to the input.
To resolve a force at an angle above the horizontal, the sine function gives the vertical component and the cosine function gives the horizontal component.
In one worked example, a 100 N force at 30 degrees has horizontal component 100 N times cos 30 degrees, 86.6 N, and vertical component 100 N times sin 30 degrees, 50.0 N.
The MCA General Engineering Science I syllabus asks candidates to resolve forces in horizontal and vertical components, restricted to the first quadrant.
The MCA Second Engineer mathematics syllabus defines sine, cosine, tangent, secant, cosecant and cotangent and the relationships between them. (added for i2, review fix)
Khan Academy's right-triangle trigonometry unit includes a lesson on the reciprocal trig ratios. (added for i2, review fix)
The two components of a vector together have the same influence as the single vector, so the vector can be replaced by its two components. (added for i2, review fix)
A projectile launched at an angle to the horizontal has an initial velocity with both a horizontal and a vertical component. (added for i2, review fix)
One field table gives conduit offset shrink of 3/16 inch per inch of offset at 30 degrees (a rounded field figure). (added for i2, review fix)
Another conduit table gives 1/4 inch (0.250) at 30 degrees, so field shrink figures at 30 degrees differ between tables (1/4 against 3/16). (added for i2, review fix)
Conduit offset shrinkage is a common field allowance, not a code rule. (added for i2, review fix)
In OpenStax Precalculus, the terminal side of an angle meets the unit circle at the point (x, y), which is equivalent to (cos t, sin t).
Sine, cosine and tangent take positive or negative values depending on the quadrant the angle is in.
A reported student error is taking the x-coordinate on the unit circle as the sine ratio, when the unit circle gives cosine as x and sine as y.
In OpenStax Precalculus, an angle measured counterclockwise from its initial side (along the positive x-axis in standard position) is a positive angle; measured clockwise, it is negative.
A reflex angle is an angle between 180° and 360°.
Angles that add together to make a straight line, 180°, are called supplementary angles.
The law of cosines says the square of any side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides minus twice their product and the cosine of the included angle.
The cosine rule can be remembered as the Pythagoras theorem with something extra so that it works for all triangles.
The cosine rule finds a missing side or angle when two sides and the included angle, or all three sides, are known.
The sine rule finds a side from another side and two angles, or an angle from two sides and a non-included angle.
With the sine rule the second possible angle is found by subtracting the first answer from 180 degrees, and exists only if the angle sum of the triangle stays within 180 degrees.

The sine rule: side a divided by the sine of angle A equals side b divided by the sine of angle B and side c divided by the sine of angle C (added in i4's review fixes, for the sine rule's general form).
One radian is the measure of a central angle of a circle that intercepts an arc equal in length to the radius of that circle.
Degree and radian measure are related by 360 degrees = 2 pi radians, or 180 degrees = pi radians.
The arc length produced by a given angle has a constant relation to the radius, whatever the length of the radius.
SQA Higher: an angle with no degree symbol is taken to be in radians.
Bird: a shaft's power is its torque times its angular speed, P = ωT.
Rotational power needs the turning speed in radians a second.
Bird's worked example: a ship's drive shaft gives a torque of 400 kN m at 400 rev/min (power 16.76 MW).
Radians are the most useful angle measure in calculus: they let the derivative rules for sine and cosine be written simply.
A sine wave can be thought of as the vertical displacement of a vector rotating at a constant speed, like the second hand of a clock, whose length is the wave's height or amplitude.
Frequency indicates how many cycles exist in one second.
A sinusoidal quantity can be written A(t) = A max sin(ωt) = A max sin(2πft).
Because the variation is sinusoidal in time, the vertical component of the rotating arrow (its magnitude times the sine of its angle with the x axis) gives v(t).
UK low-voltage supply is declared at 50 hertz unless otherwise agreed in writing.
i6: a college's marine electrical notes (SECONDARY) say 60 Hz is the most common frequency on board ship, so 60 Hz gives ω = 376.99 rad/s and a 16.7 ms period.
i6: UK mains voltages are r.m.s. values, so the declared 230 V has a peak of 230 × √2 = 325.3 V.
Phasors are good for summing sinusoids of the same frequency.
The sum of the y projections of the component phasors is the y projection of the sum of the component phasors, which is why phasor addition gives the sum wave.
Sinusoids of different frequencies cannot be shown on the same phasor diagram, because the vectors turn at different speeds.
The MCA Marine Electro-technology syllabus covers explaining phasors and solving graphical problems adding and subtracting ac voltages and currents by the phasor method.
Three-phase systems consist of three voltages equal in magnitude and 120 degrees out of phase with each other.
The square root of three in three-phase systems is a magnitude multiplier that comes from adding or subtracting two equal vectors 120 degrees apart.
At 230 V phase voltage, the three-phase line voltage is described as 400 V, not twice 230 V.
Whether a phasor's length is the peak or the rms value depends on the convention used.
notes.contested: Electronics Tutorials says a vector's magnitude is the peak value while a phasor's is the rms value; UNSW Physclips says rms phasor diagrams have the same shape as amplitude ones, scaled by 0.71.

notes.claim: i7: a college's marine electrical notes (SECONDARY) say most ships have a three-phase, three-wire 440 V supply, so a ship's 440 V between lines gives 440 ÷ √3 = 254 V a phase.
Power factor is the cosine of the angle between real power and apparent power, kW over kVA.
True power and apparent power form the adjacent and hypotenuse of a right triangle, so the power factor is the cosine of the phase angle.
In one worked 230 V example, power factor 0.6 gives a line current of 72.5 A and correcting to 0.8 reduces it to 54.5 A (source's "20 per cent" is loose: about 25 per cent).
